question_text: How many free electrons would there be in a spool of high-purity copper wire ( 1 mm diameter $\times 10 \mathrm{~m}$ long)? Give your answer as the value of free_electrons.The unit of the answer is electrons.
response:
## Reasoning

Copper is monovalent for free-electron purposes: **each Cu atom contributes 1 conduction (free) electron**. So the number of free electrons equals the number of copper atoms in the wire.

**Step 1 — Wire volume**
$$V = \pi r^{2} L = \pi(0.5\times10^{-3}\,\text{m})^{2}(10\,\text{m}) = 7.854\times10^{-6}\,\text{m}^{3}$$

**Step 2 — Mass of copper**
Using density $\rho = 8.96\,\text{g/cm}^{3} = 8960\,\text{kg/m}^{3}$:
$$m = \rho V = 8960 \times 7.854\times10^{-6} \approx 0.07036\,\text{kg} = 70.36\,\text{g}$$

**Step 3 — Moles of copper**
Molar mass $M = 63.546\,\text{g/mol}$:
$$n = \frac{70.36}{63.546} \approx 1.1075\,\text{mol}$$

**Step 4 — Number of atoms (and thus free electrons)**
$$N = n \times N_{A} = 1.1075 \times 6.022\times10^{23} \approx 6.669\times10^{23}$$

$$\boxed{6.669\times10^{23}}$$
